analysis.one_liner: Sets federal health and safety standards for residential teen treatment programs and creates a national abuse hotline.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 295-102, but the Senate Health Committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required residential programs for troubled teens — wilderness camps, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, and behavior-modification facilities — to meet minimum federal standards: banning abuse and abusive discipline, limiting restraints and seclusion, requiring criminal background checks on staff, and guaranteeing kids phone access to report abuse. It would also have created public websites listing each program's violation and death records, a national toll-free hotline, civil fines up to $50,000 per violation, and Justice Department enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Teenagers placed in residential programs for emotional, behavioral, mental-health, or substance-abuse problems, and their parents. The bill guarantees kids access to a phone and abuse hotlines, requires background-checked staff trained in abuse recognition and emergency care, bans discipline that withholds food, water, shelter, or medical care, requires prompt parent notification of investigations, and gives parents public information on each program's violation history and any child deaths [S2][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teens in residential treatment programs and their parents

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits child abuse and discipline that withholds essential food, water, clothing, shelter, or medical care, and restricts physical restraints and seclusion to the limits that apply to other community children's facilities [S2][S3][S4].

Requires FBI fingerprint and sex-offender-registry checks for every staff member and volunteer, with people convicted of child abuse, child pornography, or violent crimes barred from contact with children [S4].

Creates public websites listing each program's violations, licensing status, penalties, and any child deaths — including deaths in the five years before the bill — plus a national toll-free hotline for abuse complaints, investigated within 30 days [S2][S3][S4].
Requires parents be notified within 24 hours of changes to a child's medical treatment and within 48 hours of any on-site abuse investigation or health-and-safety violation [S4].

Conditions federal child-abuse-prevention grants on states licensing these programs, inspecting them unannounced at least every two years, and applying graduated sanctions including license revocation [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of residential teen programs bear compliance costs: background checks, staff training, licensing, unannounced inspections, public posting of their violation and death records, and civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation. Federal taxpayers fund roughly $15 million a year for oversight plus expanded child-abuse-prevention grants [S3][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Residential teen program operators and federal budgets

drawbacks.text: Smaller programs could face significant compliance and licensing costs, and some operators argued this would push programs to close or raise tuition, reducing options for families already struggling to find placement for a difficult child.

The bill shifts oversight of facilities long regulated (or not regulated) by states to the federal government, with HHS setting standards and the Justice Department empowered to sue — a real expansion of federal authority over a largely private treatment market [S2][S3][S4].
The bill attaches $235 million a year in new grant funding to the existing child-abuse-prevention program, adding to federal spending during a recession-era budget [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — banning abuse, background checks, phone access, public death records, and a hotline — address abuses that oversight of this industry had left largely unchecked, and the compliance burden falls on operators profiting from a vulnerable population. The main honest cost is that federal standards and licensing could raise operating costs for some programs, but the bill excludes state-licensed hospitals and foster homes, focusing on the poorly regulated corner of the market. The design is targeted rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 295-102 just two weeks after introduction, but the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee referred it to no action, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2011 [S6].

narrative.text: Introduced February 9, 2009 by Rep. George Miller with 23 Democratic cosponsors, the bill cleared the House Education and Labor Committee markup 32-10 two days later [S5][S6].

On February 23, 2009, the House passed it under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority — by a vote of 295 to 102, with 231 of 254 voting Democrats in favor and 64 of 178 voting Republicans [S6][S7].
The Senate received the bill the next day and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which never reported it or brought it to a vote [S4][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of residential teen treatment programs are better off: they avoided federal minimum standards, public violation and death databases, a complaint hotline, unannounced inspections, and fines up to $50,000 per violation. Families with a teen in one of these programs are correspondingly worse off.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee markup (32-10) to a House floor vote within two weeks.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill on the House floor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 24, 2009, referred it, and never reported it out or scheduled any action for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Passage was bipartisan in total (295-102) but split sharply by party: 231 of 254 voting Democrats voted yes while only 64 of 178 voting Republicans did, and the bill then died in a Senate committee with no recorded floor action.

industries.industry: Private residential teen treatment programs (therapeutic boarding schools, boot camps, wilderness and behavior-modification programs)
industries.note: The bill imposed federal minimum standards, public databases of violations and deaths, a complaint hotline, unannounced state inspections, and fines up to $50,000 per violation on these operators. Their interest in defeating it ran against the safety interests of the children in their care and their parents' ability to see program records.

The bill made states responsible for licensing, inspecting, and enforcing standards at covered programs as a condition of federal CAPTA grants — new duties but tied to $235 million a year in added grant funding.
